narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your LSAT score, your undergraduate GPA, and your grades in the third year of law school. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. At 32, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as the main reason you were more likely to struggle with the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.70 worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. Similarly, your third-year law school grades, which placed you in the fourth decile compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students, also nudged the outcome slightly toward success. However, these positive effects were not large enough to overcome the downward pressure from your LSAT score.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a meaningfully higher score would likely have the biggest impact on future applications. Consider supplementing this with targeted bar-prep resources early, so the next time you apply the prediction shifts clearly in your favor.
